correctness.rationale: All vertices communicate along the two-cycle, broadcast and return arcs. Write alpha=w/2 and e=epsilon/2. The positive right Perron vector of W/2 has equal leaf coordinates; eliminating three coordinates gives lambda(lambda^2-alpha^2)=k e^2/2, so lambda>alpha. The left side is strictly increasing above alpha, and its value at 1 exceeds k e^2/2 because 1-alpha^2-k e^2/2=1/(4k)-1/(64k^2)-1/(80000k^5)>1/(8k) for k>=4. Thus the outgoing Katz series converges. Solving c=(W/2)(1+c) gives the displayed c_a0 with numerator alpha+alpha^2+e(1+k/2)+k e^2/2<3, hence c_a0<24k. Thus c_leaf=e(1+c_a0)<1 and c_b=k(1+c_leaf)/2<k. Each cycle vertex has score at least the alternating-walk sum alpha/(1-alpha)=8k-1. Every maximizer is therefore a cycle vertex. From either such seed, nonpersistent clipping bounds the cycle mass by 2 at each positive time, b by epsilon and each leaf by epsilon (also at the first step, when the leaves are zero). The discount weights at positive times sum to one. Seed b contributes k/2 at step one alone. Dividing the uniform cycle-seed bound 2+(k+1)epsilon by k/2 gives exactly the claimed upper bound, independent of ties, which tends to zero.
residual_risks: Only the general GIP update is specialized, not the source paper's later restricted threshold schedule. Orientation is outgoing and time zero is excluded throughout.
The bound need not be tight and is vacuous at k=4; the vanishing limit is unaffected. The supplied finite trajectory test is not the infinite-time proof.

value.rationale: This is a worst-case impossibility for a named linear seed heuristic on a natural nonlinear specialization. Strong connectivity and zero lower threshold remove common degeneracies; convergence rules out failure just from using an undefined resolvent. The construction isolates recurrent reinforcement versus one-step broadcast and proves the effect for every score maximizer, not just a bad tie break or one finite example.
residual_risks: Does not address algorithms that refine the Katz seed, the authors' narrower parametric threshold choice, row-stochastic networks, or empirical prevalence.
